mcqs.question: A producer emits 5,000 messages/sec and a consumer processes 2,000/sec. What happens to the excess 3,000/sec in a durable queue with no intervention?
options: It's silently discarded by the broker
It accumulates as a growing backlog, increasing end-to-end latency for queued messages
The producer is automatically blocked from sending more
The consumer automatically spins up more instances to absorb it
mcqs.explanation: Without any backpressure strategy in place, a durable queue just keeps accepting messages, so the surplus piles up as backlog and latency grows for anything waiting behind it. Brokers don't silently drop by default, block producers, or auto-scale consumers on their own.

mcqs.question: Which backpressure strategy fits a best-effort metrics pipeline where occasional data loss is acceptable, but not an order-processing queue?
options: Slowing the producer
Buffering indefinitely
Dropping messages once a threshold is hit
Routing every message to a dead-letter queue
mcqs.explanation: Dropping is only acceptable when losing data is tolerable, which fits best-effort metrics but not orders or payments. The other options either don't address the throughput mismatch (DLQ) or aren't a data-loss trade-off at all.

mcqs.question: During an outage, a consumer retries every failed message instantly with no delay. What's the risk?
options: The consumer will run out of memory immediately
Messages will be processed out of order permanently
The dead-letter queue will fill up faster than intended
A retry storm — retry volume can exceed the original load and amplify the outage
mcqs.explanation: Instant, unbounded retries pile on top of an already-failing system, which is the definition of a retry storm and can make recovery take longer, not shorter. It's not primarily a memory or ordering issue, and it doesn't directly cause the DLQ to overfill.

mcqs.question: A consumer is configured to retry a message up to 5 times. On the 6th failure, what should happen?
options: The broker routes the message to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying again
The message is silently discarded with no record
The entire queue is paused until someone intervenes
The consumer keeps retrying indefinitely until it succeeds
mcqs.explanation: Once the retry cap is hit, moving the message to a DLQ keeps it visible for investigation without blocking the rest of the queue or retrying forever. Silent discard loses the message with no trace, and pausing the whole queue over one bad message is unnecessary.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference in outcome between immediate retries and retry with exponential backoff during a real downstream outage?
options: Immediate retries always resolve the outage faster
Backoff tapers retry volume over time, giving the failing system room to recover, while immediate retries can compound the load and worsen the outage
There's no practical difference once a dead-letter queue is in place
Backoff guarantees zero message loss while immediate retry guarantees message loss
mcqs.explanation: Backoff spaces out retries so the struggling system gets breathing room to recover, whereas immediate retries can pile on faster than the system can absorb, prolonging the outage. A DLQ handles messages that exceed the retry cap but doesn't change the retry-volume dynamics themselves, and message-loss guarantees aren't inherent to either strategy.
